newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends down in U.S., eyes retail sales, crosses.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends down in U.S., eyes retail sales, crosses.

text.p: The dollar ended weaker versus the mark and yen partly after a report showing weaker U.S. retail sales briefly dimmed hopes for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike next week, currency experts said.
Another catalyst for dollar declines against the yen emerged as the Japanese currency strengthened versus the mark, they said.

The Commerce Department said total retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April, the largest drop since a 0.5 percent decline last June. Excluding autos, sales slid 0.1 percent in April instead of rising 0.1 percent as expected in a Reuter poll.
Retail sales for March were also revised lower.

Currency traders are keeping a close watch on a barrage of key U.S. economic data due out this week for any clues about whether the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will decide to tighten credit again when it meets again on May 20.
Fed policymakers had hiked the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.

"The market partly expected that the Fed might stay on hold in the coming FOMC. That's the reason for some dip in the dollar just after the retail sales report," said Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.
The dollar closed at 118.55/65 yen and 1.6930/40 marks, down from 119.10/20 yen and 1.6985/95 marks at the open.
Meanwhile, the mark traded near 69.87/92 yen in late dealings, down from around 70.17/20 in very early activity.

Retail sales will be followed by the release of the producer prices index (PPI) on Wednesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, expected the PPI to be unchanged in April but up 0.1 percent in the core, which excludes volatile food and energy items.
The PPI fell 0.1 percent in March, while the core climbed 0.4 percent.
In other trade, the British pound strengthened after a Bank of England quarterly report on inflation stated that interest rates need to rise further in Britain.

The central bank report said monetary policy needs to be tightened further if the nation is to hit the inflation target of 2.5 percent or lower in the medium term. It warned that inflation is more likely than not to exceed the target in two years or so unless action is taken to slow the pace of the economic expansion.
The pound finished at $1.6317/27, up from $1.6237/47.

Britain's new Labour government had surprised financial markets last week by transferring operational responsibility for setting interest rates to the Bank of England. Short-term rates were also hiked to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent.

The Bank of England's "independence itself is a good psychological boost for sterling and then comments like that that indicate they're going to be aggressive against inflation is also helping sterling," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank.
During overnight trading, remarks from senior Japanese officials had rippled through currency markets.

Bank of Japan executive director Yutaka Yamaguchi told a parliamentary committee in Tokyo on Tuesday that a rise in Japan's long-term interest rates reflects a brighter outlook by financial markets on the Japanese economy.

"Clearly, they're looking for a stronger Japanese economy later this year and higher rates will naturally follow and that should benefit the yen," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 1.4355/65 Swiss francs from 1.4340/50. It fell to Canadian $1.3858/63 from C$1.3863/68. The Australian dollar slid to $0.7760/65 from $0.7786/91.

Yamaguchi also said it was important for currency rates to stabilize at levels that reflected economic fundamentals of the countries concerned. This sentiment was echoed by Japanese finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who said foreign exchange rates were likely to settle at an appropriate level soon.
